newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU cereal cuts, beef label plans set for bashing.
newsitem.headline: EU cereal cuts, beef label plans set for bashing.

text.p: European Commission proposals, slashing aid to cereal and oilseed farmers and making beef labelling compulsory, are expected to be strongly attacked by EU farm ministers next week.

EU diplomats said France and Germany are set to lead the attack at a meeting starting on Monday that could continue until Wednesday as countries protest against a fresh attempt to cut cereals and oilseeds aids by 1.4 billion ecus.

Member states are also angry that European Commission President Jacques Santer has apparently caved in to pressure from the European Parliament to give it a joint say on EU-wide cattle tracing and compulsory beef labelling systems
"Most ministers are irritated and ready to let off a lot of steam," one diplomat said, adding that beef labelling, aimed at restoring consumer confidence after the mad cow crisis.
It could be delayed months although the Commission, the Parliament and member states agree action is urgently needed.

On cereal cuts, part of the 1997/98 farm price package, member states are sceptical about European Commission budgetary forecasts after it recently slashed 1.1 billion ecus off planned savings to meet tight 1998 budget targets for a single currency.

When the Commission last summer made an identical proposal to cut cereals aid in order to finance an emergency beef aid package after the mad cow crisis, it was only supported only by Britain, Sweden and Denmark and quietly dropped.
Funds to aid beef farmers were found by partly postponing oilseed aid payments until the next financial year.

On cattle identification and beef labelling, the European Commission last week presented a revised proposal combining the two scheme, giving the European Parliament joint decision-making power and making beef labelling compulsory from January, 2000.

Apart from fiercely resisting greater European Parliament involvement and subsequent loss of national sovereignty, several countries -- Britain, Ireland, Italy, Denmark and Spain -- also reject compulsory labelling, saying it would distort trade.
The label would specify the regions in which cattle were born, fattened and slaughtered as well as feeding data, but would not reveal the country of origin.

Diplomats said agreement was close on an EU-wide cattle identification network consisting of national computerised data bases and passports for each animal so that their movements can be traced from birth.
"But there's a big cleavage on labelling," one noted.
On Monday, the Dutch EU Presidency will try to make progress by seeing if there is the necessary unanimous agreement to reject the Commission's proposal.
"It's theoretically possible to get (unanimous) agreement on identification based on article 43 a of the treaty (consultation of parliament," a diplomat said
